title: What To Do If You Work For a Micromanager
author: Houston, Parker
summary: Parker Houston uses the story of Clint, who quit under his micromanaging boss Jack, to illustrate micromanagement dynamics. Jack checked constantly, revised Clint's work until none remained original, and undermined autonomy despite demanding it. Houston identifies seven roots of micromanagement (fear of control loss, insecurity, perfectionism, pressure from above, low trust, worry about competence, lack of exposure to better models) and acknowledges most are anxiety-reduction strategies rooted in childhood. For employees: be competent, clarify deliverables upfront, schedule regular updates, explain reasoning, offer options, focus on your own behavior, and quit if toxic. The critical insight: you cannot change the micromanager, but you can manage your response.
points: Jack's friendly demeanor masked deep anxiety about control: constant checking, work revision until unrecognizable, and requiring permission for small decisions sent the message Take full ownership, but run everything by me first, creating suffocation.
Micromanagement roots are deep: fear of control loss, insecurity, perfectionism, pressure from above are anxiety strategies rooted in childhood, rarely amenable to external change.
Practical interventions: proactively clarify deliverables, schedule regular project updates to pre-empt checking, explain reasoning, offer upfront control through options.
Do not try to change the micromanager; focus on your own behavior and seeing their good qualities, or their defensiveness will intensify.
If months of adjustment don't reduce toxicity, recognize poor fit and quit: this is about your health and wellbeing, not organizational loyalty.
quotes: Jack continued to delegate tasks and then take them back if they were not done immediately.
Clint was a competent worker who had rapidly promoted, a strong leader, and highly reliable—he was not being micromanaged due to incompetence.
It's critical that your response to micromanagement be realistic, and primarily focus on how you manage yourself in response to their style.
Ultimately, micromanagers may be dealing with anxiety management strategies that originated in childhood and may have been part of their way of doing things for the better part of a century.
If you try for months to adjust to their style and you are still too frustrated at work, you may need to change jobs.
